channel.title: Solar & Geomagnetic Alerts
channel.description: Significant solar flares, solar eruptions, geomagnetic storms, radiation storms, solar wind shocks and power-grid risk. WATCH = worth keeping an eye on; WARNING = a significant event is likely or under way; ALERT = an extreme event. Times are UTC.

item.title: WATCH: Sunspot AR4566 update, now also: has already produced strong flares
item.description: Sunspot region AR4566 (at S06E06 on the Sun, facing Earth) was already flagged as potentially dangerous and now also has: it has already produced 1 medium or strong (M or X class) flare. item.title: ALERT: Very rapid magnetic field change in Europe: 1038 nT/min measured at Nurmijarvi, Finland (NUR); risk of currents in power grids
item.description: Very rapid magnetic field change in Europe: 1038 nT/min measured at Nurmijarvi, Finland (NUR); risk of currents in power grids. Level: ALERT (the ALERT threshold is 800 nT/min). The peak was 1038 nT/min at 2026-11-06 08:45 UTC; it began at 08:45 UTC. This is how fast the horizontal magnetic field changed, in nanotesla per minute (nT/min), measured by ground observatories in Europe; on quiet days it is usually only a few nT/min or less. Why it matters: fast changes in Earth's magnetic field drive electric currents through the ground and into long conductors such as power lines, pipelines and railway circuits (geomagnetically induced currents). Strong ones can trip protection equipment, cause voltage problems or overheat transformers; the Quebec blackout of March 1989 was caused this way. Whether a particular grid is affected depends on the grid and the local rock beneath it.

item.title: WARNING: Strong electric field in the ground across the US and Canada: 1207 mV/km near 60.0°N 109.5°W; risk of currents in power grids
item.description: Strong electric field in the ground across the US and Canada: 1207 mV/km near 60.0°N 109.5°W; risk of currents in power grids. Level: WARNING (the WARNING threshold is 1000 mV/km). The peak was 1207 mV/km at 2026-11-04 07:51 UTC; it began at 07:51 UTC. This is the electric field in the ground, in millivolts per kilometre (mV/km), from NOAA's geoelectric field model for the US and Canada; values this high are far above normal. The value shown was reached or exceeded at 3 grid points, so one odd point cannot trigger an alert. Why it matters: fast changes in Earth's magnetic field drive electric currents through the ground and into long conductors such as power lines, pipelines and railway circuits (geomagnetically induced currents). Strong ones can trip protection equipment, cause voltage problems or overheat transformers; the Quebec blackout of March 1989 was caused this way. Whether a particular grid is affected depends on the grid and the local rock beneath it.
